Spat
SPAT
v. (past tense of spit; cast spittle)
Past tense of spit, Old English spittan, of imitative origin. The Greek ptuo is likewise imitative. Mark uses the related form spit in his parallel healings.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

The healing of the man born blind begins with the most undignified act in the Gospels: “When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay” (John 9:6). The Creator stoops, spat, mixes earth with His own spittle and puts it on a man's eyes. The echo of Genesis is unmistakable: the hands that formed Adam of the dust of the ground form eyes of clay for a man who had never had sight. And the cure required obedience before it gave light: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing” (John 9:7). Mark records the same method with another man: “And he took the blind man by the hand, and led him out of the town; and when he had spit on his eyes, and put his hands upon him, he asked him if he saw ought” (Mark 8:23). The Lord who received spitting in His face at His trial gave sight by His own spittle. Nothing in the incarnation is too lowly for Him to use.

Webster 1828 Definition

Greek ptuo, to spit, of imitative origin.

Joh 9:7 — "And said unto him, Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing."

Modern Corruption

The physical means in Christ's healings are either read as folk magic or spiritualised away, when they display the dignity of His true humanity and the sovereignty of His method.

expand to see more

Two readings miss this verse from opposite sides. Comparative-religion treatments file the clay and spittle with ancient healing magic, as though Christ were employing a technique whose power lay in the materials. And a certain docetic squeamishness in the church, uncomfortable with so bodily an act from the Son of God, hurries past the spittle to the lesson.

Both lose the doctrine. Chalcedonian Christology holds one Person in two natures, truly God and truly man, without confusion or division; the spittle is the Son of God's own, and it heals because of who He is, not because of what it is. He healed elsewhere by a word at a distance, which forecloses any magic in the mud. And the method preaches: the Maker of Adam from dust makes eyes from clay, sends the man to the pool called Sent, and gives light through obedience.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Past tense of spit, Old English spittan; Greek ptuo; John 9:6 has Christ making clay of His own spittle.

expand to see more

Old English spittan, to spit, of imitative origin; spat is its past tense.

Greek ptuo, likewise imitative.

John 9:6 is the only occurrence of spat in the Authorized Version.

The Maker of Adam from dust forms eyes of clay.

The pool of Siloam means Sent, and the cure came through obedience.
